result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch02-discrete-time-models status: complete --- # Discrete-time models {#sec-discrete-time-models} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 1, Session 3. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd). ::: Many epidemic data arrive in discrete intervals — daily case counts, weekly reports — and many simulations advance in fixed steps. This chapter develops the discrete-time SIR model in two flavours: a **deterministic function map** with continuous state, and a **stochastic Markov chain** with integer counts. We then show that as the step width $\delta t$ shrinks, the deterministic map converges to the continuous ODE of @sec-foundations, tying the discrete and continuous worlds together. ## Learning goals By the end of this chapter you should be able to: - write a discrete-time SIR update using the rate-to-proportion conversion; - contrast the deterministic map with the binomial Markov chain of @sec-probability-and-stochastic-processes; - run a stochastic ensemble and compare its mean with the deterministic map; - demonstrate numerically that the map converges to the ODE as $\delta t \to 0$; - verify population conservation in both formulations. ## Model assumptions and classification All three models share the SIR assumptions of @sec-foundations — closed, well-mixed population, mass-action transmission, constant recovery. They differ only in how they represent time and state: | Model | Determinism | Time | State | |---|---|---|---| | Function map | Deterministic | Discrete | Continuous | | Markov chain | Stochastic | Discrete | Discrete (integer) | | ODE (@sec-foundations) | Deterministic | Continuous | Continuous | The function map is the deterministic *expectation* of the Markov chain: it moves the mean number of individuals each step, whereas the chain draws a random integer around that mean. ## Equations Over a step of width $\delta t$, the per-capita probabilities of infection and recovery are obtained from the continuous rates via the Poisson conversion introduced in @eq-p01-rate: $$ p_I = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta c I_t}{N}\,\delta t\right), \qquad p_R = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\gamma\,\delta t\right). $$ {#eq-ch02-probs} The **deterministic map** moves the expected number of individuals: $$ \begin{aligned} S_{t+1} &= S_t - p_I S_t,\\ I_{t+1} &= I_t + p_I S_t - p_R I_t,\\ R_{t+1} &= R_t + p_R I_t. \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-ch02-map} The **stochastic chain** replaces those expectations with binomial draws (cf. @eq-p02-chain): $$ Y_t \sim \text{Binomial}(S_t, p_I), \quad Z_t \sim \text{Binomial}(I_t, p_R), \quad \begin{aligned} S_{t+1} &= S_t - Y_t,\\ I_{t+1} &= I_t + Y_t - Z_t,\\ R_{t+1} &= R_t + Z_t. \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-ch02-chain} As $\delta t \to 0$, $p_I \to \tfrac{\beta c I}{N}\delta t$ and $p_R \to \gamma\,\delta t$, so the map @eq-ch02-map reduces to a forward-Euler step of the ODE @eq-ch01-sir and converges to it. ## Julia implementation The two kernels sit side by side so the only difference — deterministic movement versus a binomial draw — is explicit. ::: {#cell-ch02-kernels .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Distributions, StableRNGs rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt) function sir_map_step(state, p, δt) # deterministic, eq-ch02-map S, I, R = state β, c, γ, N = p infection = rate_to_proportion(β * c * I / N, δt) * S recovery = rate_to_proportion(γ, δt) * I return (S - infection, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery) end function sir_chain_step(state, p, δt, rng) # stochastic, eq-ch02-chain S, I, R = state β, c, γ, N = p Y = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, S), rate_to_proportion(β * c * I / N, δt))) Z = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, I), rate_to_proportion(γ, δt))) return (S - Y, I + Y - Z, R + Z) end function iterate_model(step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = ()) traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, nsteps + 1) traj[:, 1] .= u0 state = Tuple(float.(u0)) for k in 1:nsteps state = step(state, p, δt, extra...) traj[:, k + 1] .= state end return traj end ``` ::: {#ch02-kernels .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` iterate_model (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: We run the deterministic map and a 200-member stochastic ensemble on the baseline scenario with $\delta t = 1$ day. ::: {#cell-ch02-run .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} u0 = [990, 10, 0] p = (0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000.0) δt = 1.0 nsteps = 40 ts = 0:nsteps map_traj = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> sir_map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, nsteps) nsims = 200 chain_ens = [iterate_model(sir_chain_step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = (StableRNG(seed),)) for seed in 1:nsims] chain_I = reduce(hcat, (traj[2, :] for traj in chain_ens)) chain_mean_I = vec(sum(chain_I; dims = 2)) ./ nsims (round(maximum(map_traj[2, :]); digits = 1), round(maximum(chain_mean_I); digits = 1)) ``` ::: {#ch02-run .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (200.9, 190.8) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch02-compare .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie fig = Figure(size = (720, 440)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)", title = "Discrete-time SIR: map vs stochastic chain (δt = 1)") for j in 1:nsims lines!(ax, ts, chain_I[:, j]; color = (:grey, 0.12), linewidth = 1) end lines!(ax, ts, chain_mean_I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "chain mean") lines!(ax, ts, map_traj[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 3, label = "function map") axislegend(ax; position = :rt) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch02-compare .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Infectious compartment: stochastic Markov-chain realisations (thin grey), their ensemble mean (red), and the deterministic function map (dashed black). The map closely tracks the stochastic mean. ::: ::: ### Convergence of the map to the ODE As $\delta t \to 0$ the deterministic map should approach the continuous-time ODE solution. We compare the map at the fixed horizon $t = 40$ against a high-accuracy `Tsit5` reference across a sequence of shrinking steps. ::: {#cell-ch02-convergence .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using OrdinaryDiffEq function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t) S, I, R = u β, c, γ, N = p λ = β * c * I / N du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - γ * I; du[3] = γ * I return nothing end tmax = 40.0 ode_ref = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, float.(u0), (0.0, tmax), p), Tsit5(); reltol = 1e-12, abstol = 1e-12, save_everystep = false).u[end] δts = [tmax / 2^k for k in 5:13] map_errors = map(δts) do dt n = round(Int, tmax / dt) traj = iterate_model((s, p, d) -> sir_map_step(s, p, d), u0, p, dt, n) maximum(abs.(traj[:, end] .- ode_ref)) end [(round(dt; sigdigits = 3), round(err; sigdigits = 3)) for (dt, err) in zip(δts, map_errors)] ``` ::: {#ch02-convergence .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 9-element Vector{Tuple{Float64, Float64}}: (1.25, 71.3) (0.625, 39.2) (0.312, 20.6) (0.156, 10.6) (0.0781, 5.34) (0.0391, 2.69) (0.0195, 1.35) (0.00977, 0.675) (0.00488, 0.338) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ch02-convergence .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig2 = Figure(size = (640, 420)) ax2 = Axis(fig2[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "step size δt", ylabel = "‖map − ODE‖ at t = 40", title = "Map → ODE convergence") scatter!(ax2, δts, map_errors; markersize = 12, color = :steelblue, label = "measured") guide = map_errors[1] .* (δts ./ δts[1]) lines!(ax2, δts, guide; linestyle = :dash, color = :black, label = "slope 1") axislegend(ax2; position = :rb) fig2 ``` ::: {#fig-ch02-convergence .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Error of the deterministic map at $t=40$ relative to the ODE solution, versus step size (log–log). The points parallel the slope-1 guide, confirming first-order convergence of the map to the ODE. ::: ::: ## Validation **Conservation.** Both the deterministic map and every stochastic realisation must keep the population at $N = 1000$: ::: {#cell-ch02-check-conservation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} map_ok = all(k -> isapprox(sum(map_traj[:, k]), 1000.0; atol = 1e-8), 1:nsteps+1) chain_ok = all(traj -> all(k -> sum(traj[:, k]) == 1000, 1:nsteps+1), chain_ens) (map_ok, chain_ok) ``` ::: {#ch02-check-conservation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (true, true) ``` ::: ::: **Convergence.** The empirical order of the map-to-ODE error should be close to 1, matching the forward-Euler analysis of @sec-calculus-and-numerical-methods: ::: {#cell-ch02-check-order .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} orders = [log2(map_errors[k] / map_errors[k+1]) for k in 1:length(map_errors)-1] mean_order = sum(orders) / length(orders) (round(mean_order; digits = 3), isapprox(mean_order, 1.0; atol = 0.1)) ``` ::: {#ch02-check-order .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.965, true) ``` ::: ::: Both cells confirm the expected behaviour: population is conserved in every trajectory, and the map converges to the ODE at first order. ## Interpretation and limitations The three models form a coherent family. The Markov chain is the most faithful: it produces integer counts, allows an epidemic to fade out by chance, and shows run-to-run variability that shrinks as the population grows. The deterministic map is its mean-field shadow — cheap and smooth, but blind to extinction and fluctuations. Both are only *approximations* to the continuous process, exact only as $\delta t \to 0$; at $\delta t = 1$ day the discretisation error is visible but modest. A subtle limitation of the binomial construction is that it processes all infections and recoveries within a step simultaneously, so an individual cannot become infected *and* recover in the same step — an artefact that vanishes as the step shrinks. The exact event-driven treatment is the subject of the continuous-time Markov chain chapter. See the [Distributions.jl documentation](https://juliastats.org/Distributions.jl/stable/) and the [SciML FunctionMap solver](https://docs.sciml.ai/OrdinaryDiffEq/stable/) for the corresponding library tools. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch02-ex1} Run the stochastic chain ensemble at $\delta t = 1$ and again at $\delta t = 0.25$ (with the horizon fixed at 40 days). Compare the ensemble-mean infectious peak against the deterministic map at each step size, and explain which discretisation sits closer to the ODE reference and why. ### Exercise 2 {#ch02-ex2} Compute, from the 200-member ensemble, the probability that the epidemic goes extinct (reaches $I = 0$) before day 40 for the baseline $R_0 = 2$. Then lower the contact rate to $c = 6$ and recompute. Explain the change in terms of the reproduction number and demographic stochasticity — a phenomenon the deterministic map cannot capture. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/02-discrete-time-models.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/02-discrete-time-models.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/02-discrete-time-models.jl)
